items.label: Blogs

🫧 Open on Bubbles

It's only a few weeks until the winter solstice—the shortest day of the year. Right now, we only get eight hours of daylight per day up here, as well as over 20cm of snow in a few days after weeks of blonde grass and warm chinook winds. Solstice represents a turning point toward light, hope, fresh starts, and a new cycle, sure. But it's dark right now. It's dark, but I want it darker.

You see, in addition to finishing the curation and compilation of the work I've been doing for the past year into a couple books, I also took a few days to set up an "in case of emergency" USB stick. It's a ~100 GB stick built for three situations: emergency reference, rebuilding after losing every computer I own, and a handoff for my family if something happens to me. There's a plain-text START HERE.txt file explaining everything, and it's all just files that open in a browser or editor. Many of us will have been asked by others to pray for them, or may have taken it upon ourselves to do so, particularly where they have no belief in God. We probably find, over time, that this turns into a 'wish' list that gets longer and longer, leaving less and less time for quiet prayer.

Do we need to use these lists though, sometimes verbalised out loud. It reminds me a little bit of a small section of a film I saw where someone asked a Greek orthodox monk to pray for them and he replied 'I already do'. The person was naturally confused and asked how he could as he hadn't known him until that moment. The monk replied that he prayed for the whole world, and wasn't he a part of that?

It is important to remember that, when we pray, we are not trying to bring God's love to us or those around us. It is already there. The 'list prayers' then, are probably at least partly for our benefit as much as anyone else's .. to think that we are taking action to help others.

items.title: Trafalgar Square's Christmas tree is on its way to London after being felled in a forest north of Oslo yesterday morning, accompanied by Norwegian Christmas carols
items.label: Hobbies and Creative
items.excerpt:
Published on 20th November 2026 by Ian Mansfield in London News

Trafalgar Square’s Christmas tree is on its way to London after being felled in a forest north of Oslo this morning, accompanied by Norwegian Christmas carols.

The Trafalgar Square Tree tradition is now in its 79th year and is a symbol of gratitude following the Second World War, when King Haakon VII of Norway sought refuge in Britain and the Norwegian government-in-exile was based in London. In recognition of that act, Norway has sent a Christmas tree to London every year since 1947.

This year’s tree grew in the woods at Høgåsen in Sørkedalen, a few miles north of Oslo, and was chosen from a short list of three following a public vote in Oslo. The 21-metre-tall Norwegian spruce (Picea abies) was about 75 years old, and this morning it was felled by the Lord Mayor of Westminster, Cllr Karen Scarborough, along with the Mayor of Oslo, Anne Lindboe.

items.title: I tried to listen to music
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
Sometimes online, I stumble upon posts of people born before music streaming was a thing and they explain how listening to new music back then was an experience.

They would go to the shop, buy a CD or vinyl after struggling to choose. Then they'd come home, and listen to the music they had just bought. Nothing more, simply sitting there and listening.

This is really foreign to me as I've always seen music as a commodity. Music is the thing you put in the car, while washing the dishes, when you have a long walk to go somewhere, what's on at the radio when you're grocery shopping.

It is never about the music itself, more like an enjoyable background noise that you pay some attention to, but never all your attention.

And it makes sense that it works that way for me, because music has always been so easily available in nearly infinite quantities so it seems like a nice but unimportant thing.

I recently gave the opening talk at Swift Bharat 2026 in Mumbai, India.

I had spent MONTHS trying to figure out what I wanted to talk about.

I’ve been programming since 2004, building iOS apps since 2010, and giving technical talks for years. I’ve worked on fastlane, spent years helping developers ship software, organized Deep Dish Swift, and given more technical talks than I can probably remember.

And apparently it took me several months and a ridiculous number of slide revisions to figure that out. 😅

items.excerpt:
You struck a deal with a dragon: twenty years of protection for twenty years of dinner service. The island thrives under the beast's watchful eye, as long as the meals keep coming.

Every year, the dragon wakes up hungrier. You roll dice to work your island, harvest ingredients, fuse them into recipes, and cook them down in the Scorchpot — the pot you keep full or end up in. Get the meal right and you prosper. Get it wrong and you're smoke.

Build farmsteads, shrines, and harbors across your hex-grid island, each one changing how the board pays out. The best runs start with a handful of tiles and end with a machine that buries the dragon in food. Then the odds tighten, the dragon turns picky, and you tear the whole thing down and rebuild while it's on fire.

Feed the Scorchpot, keep the dragon happy, and outlast the contract.
